 ‘Yes on 5’ concedes in apparent defeat of tax refund question
 Share
 Email 
 Facebook 
 Twitter 
 This year’s Ballot Question 5 asked voters whether to update the state’s law that caps revenue. 
 boonchai wedmakawand/Getty Images
 Moment RF
 Diane Adame
 dianeaadame 
 diane.adame@gbh.org 
 Diane Adame is digital reporter with GBH News. Feedback? Questions? Story ideas? Reach out to Diane at diane.adame@gbh.org. 
 November 04, 2026
 While the race for Ballot Question 5 has yet to be officially called, the campaign behind the measure intended to limit state revenues and create more frequent tax refunds conceded Wednesday morning. This year’s Ballot Question 5 asked voters whether to update the state’s law that caps revenue.
 “It’s clear that Massachusetts voters want a well-funded government that’s capable of investing in families to create broadly shared prosperity,” said Harris Gruman, chair of Protect Massachusetts Future, which opposed the measure. “The solution to our affordability woes is adequate funding for state programs that reduce costs for workers, families, and seniors; not indiscriminate budget-cutting that leaves us all worse off.”
 Massachusetts taxpayers were asked to weigh in on a record-tying nine ballot questions Tuesday, opting to keep recreational cannabis legal, make public records laws more expansive, allow same-day voter registration on Election Day and preserving gun restrictions.

 But a couple of results had not yet been called by midday Wednesday. 
 Massachusetts has had a law on the books for 40 years that requires the state to return some revenue to residents when tax collections outpace wage growth. Taxpayers have received refunds just twice under the current formula since the law was first passed in 1986.

 Question 5 would have altered how the state calculates its thresholds for tax refunds. The new formula would tie the ceiling directly to the prior year’s actual revenue collections plus wage growth. 
 Taxpayers for an Affordable Massachusetts, the group behind the measure, said they are disappointed by the defeat and respect the voters’ decision. But they emphasize that important questions remain about “the growth of state spending, the cost of living and doing business, and Massachusetts’ ability to retain residents, jobs, and investment.” 
 “Question 5 proposed modernizing the state’s nearly 40-year-old revenue growth limit by connecting allowable tax collections more directly to the growth of Massachusetts wages and salaries,” Chris Keohan, a spokesperson for the group, said in a statement. “The campaign brought this issue into a statewide debate about government spending, taxpayer refunds, and the economic pressures facing Massachusetts residents and employers.”
 The Pioneer Institute is one of the groups that supported the measure, which executive director Jim Stergios said was always meant to “provide modest help with affordability, without forcing cuts in state services.”

 “Reading this morning’s electoral map, it turns out Question 5 is a proof point for the growing divide in Massachusetts politics between the wealthy, liberal communities that voted against it and working-class cities voted for it,” he said in a statement. “Classic have and have-nots split, with a pinch of paternalism.”
 Stergois said that “voters in Cambridge, Newton, Brookline and Somerville don’t feel that an average rebate of $700 is meaningful, but voters in Springfield, New Bedford, Chicopee, and Lawrence beg to differ.”
 In a statement, Gruman said Massachusetts voters made it clear that protecting essential state investments in health care, education, housing and local aid matters more than limiting public spending. 
 “Now, as Massachusetts faces billions of dollars in federal budget cuts to healthcare and food assistance, we need to listen to the voters who asked the top 1% to pay their fair share four years ago, and rejected strict state revenue limits this year,” he wrote. “Voters want Massachusetts to ensure that the wealthy individuals and big corporations who have seen their profits skyrocket pay their fair share, so we can build a fair economy that works for all of us.”
